# Framework (Privacy-First Mode)
# ================================================================================
# This project uses Framework's privacy-first structure.
# All */private/ directories are gitignored by default.
# Only */public/ directories can be committed after explicit review.
#
# WORKFLOW:
#   1. Sensitive/raw data goes in */private/ directories (NEVER committed)
#   2. De-identified/aggregated data goes in */public/ directories (safe to commit)
#   3. Analysis scripts are committed, but outputs are carefully controlled
#
# CRITICAL: Private directories are NEVER committed to version control.
# ================================================================================

# ============================================================================
# SENSITIVE DATA - NEVER COMMIT
# ============================================================================

# Private directories - explicit paths for this project type
/inputs/private/
/reference/private/
/outputs/private/

# Generic private directory patterns (defense-in-depth)
**/private/**
**/*_private/**
**/sensitive/**

# Allow structure documentation (README and .gitkeep files in private dirs)
!/inputs/**/README.md
!/inputs/**/.gitkeep
!/reference/**/README.md
!/reference/**/.gitkeep
!/outputs/**/README.md
!/outputs/**/.gitkeep

# ============================================================================
# SECRETS AND CREDENTIALS - NEVER COMMIT
# ============================================================================

.env
.env.local
.env.*.local
.Renviron
.httr-oauth
**/credentials/**
**/secrets/**
*.key
*.pem
*.p12
*.pfx

# ============================================================================
# UTILITY & CACHE - SAFE TO IGNORE
# ============================================================================

# Temporary processing directories
**/cache/**
**/scratch/**
**/tmp/**
**/temp/**

# Logs (run logs, cluster job output)
**/logs/**
slurm-*.out

# ============================================================================
# FRAMEWORK INTERNALS
# ============================================================================

framework.db
framework.db-wal
framework.db-shm
.initiated
.framework_scaffolded

# ============================================================================
# QUARTO ARTIFACTS
# ============================================================================

# Quarto adds these two lines, in this form, unless they are here already
/.quarto/
**/*.quarto_ipynb
# A folder with its own _quarto.yml gets its own .quarto/
.quarto/
_freeze/
# Backups from quarto_regenerate() before framework-py 0.1.0.dev13
.quarto_backups/
*_cache/
*_files/

# ============================================================================
# PYTHON ENVIRONMENT
# ============================================================================

__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.venv/
venv/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
.pytest_cache/
.mypy_cache/
.ruff_cache/
*.egg-info/
build/
dist/

# ============================================================================
# IDE & SYSTEM FILES
# ============================================================================

# IDE - personal settings only (commit workspace settings if desired)
.idea/
.vscode/.history/
.positron/.history/
.history/

# macOS
.DS_Store
.AppleDouble
.LSOverride

# Windows
Thumbs.db
ehthumbs.db

# Linux
*~

# ============================================================================
# CLOUD/AWS CONFIG
# ============================================================================

.aws/
.config/

# ============================================================================
# TEMPORARY FILES
# ============================================================================

*.tmp
*.log
*.bak
*.swp
*~

# --- from base framework/project_sensitive v5 ---
# Private data and credentials
**/private/**
**/*_private/**
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
.Renviron
**/credentials/**
**/secrets/**

# Local records and caches
framework.db
framework.db-wal
framework.db-shm
.DS_Store

# Sensitive project folders
/inputs/private/
/reference/private/
/outputs/private/
**/sensitive/**

# Run logs
/logs/

matplotlib-figures.content:
---
name: matplotlib-figures
description: Use when making a matplotlib or seaborn figure in Python, from a quick look at the data to a figure for a paper, report, poster, or slides. Covers choosing the chart, accurate defaults, titles and labels, accessible color, honest scales, styles, and saving.
metadata:
  title: Figures with matplotlib
  summary: Accurate matplotlib and seaborn figures, from exploring data to publication.
---

# Figures with matplotlib

## Chart choice

Values on a shared axis are the easiest to compare.

| Question | Chart | seaborn or matplotlib |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution of one numeric variable | Histogram | `sns.histplot()` |
| A numeric variable across groups | Box plot with the points | `sns.boxplot()`, `sns.stripplot()` |
| Counts by category | Bar chart, sorted | `sns.countplot()`, `ax.barh()` |
| Two numeric variables | Scatterplot | `sns.scatterplot()`, `sns.regplot()` |
| Change over time or another ordered variable | Line chart | `sns.lineplot()` |
| A pattern across subgroups | Small multiples | `sns.relplot(col=...)`, `sns.catplot(col=...)` |

Avoid dual y axes and 3-D effects. In a stacked bar, only the bottom segment
sits on a shared baseline.

## Accuracy

- **Histograms:** try more than one bin width. Set `binwidth` in the units of
  the variable.
- **Group summaries:** a box plot hides group size and multiple peaks. With a
  few hundred points or fewer, overlay them with
  `sns.stripplot(..., alpha=0.3)`.
- **Overplotting:** lower `alpha`, use smaller markers, or pass both `x` and
  `y` to `sns.histplot()` for a 2-D histogram.
- **Skewed variables:** use `ax.set_xscale("log")` or `ax.set_yscale("log")`
  for strongly right-skewed values. Say so in the axis label.
- **Bars:** a bar's length encodes its value, so the axis starts at zero. Use
  points when zero is not meaningful.
- **Order:** sort categories by value unless they have a natural order.
- **Missing-value codes:** check the codebook for codes such as -99 before
  plotting, and recode them to missing.
- **Missing values:** seaborn drops rows with missing values without a
  warning. Count them with `df[cols].isna().sum()` before you trust the
  figure.
- **Panels:** panels that readers compare share axis limits, with
  `sharex=True` and `sharey=True`. Free scales suit panels not meant to be
  compared. Say so in the caption.

## Titles and labels

- **Axes:** use plain names with units, such as "Income per person (US
  dollars, log scale)". Replace column names such as `sbp_mean`.
- **Title:** a title that states the finding, such as "Blood pressure rises
  with age in every group", can help a figure communicate its result. Make
  sure it suits the venue. Some journals and readers prefer a matter-of-fact
  title that names the variables, such as "Systolic blood pressure by age".
  Follow the venue's style, and ask the user when it is unclear. Do not
  invent a finding.
- **Subtitle and caption:** say what is measured, for whom, and when. Give
  the data source, the sample size, and caveats such as the handling of
  missing values.
- **Direct labels:** with a few series, label lines or points directly with
  `ax.annotate()` or `ax.text()` and remove the legend.
- **Uncertainty:** show it with the same method and interval level as the
  analysis. Label a confidence interval as uncertainty in the estimate.

## Color

- For categories, use a palette readable with color vision deficiency, such
  as `sns.color_palette("colorblind")` or viridis. For ordered values, use
  viridis or a single-hue sequential palette.
- Pair color with labels, position, marker shape, or line style, so the figure
  still works in grayscale.

## Styles

A shared style is a good tactic when a project makes many figures. It keeps
them consistent and saves repeating the same settings. Define it once, as a
style sheet or a function that sets `rcParams`, and apply it to each figure.
If the project already has a style, use it. A one-off figure can set its style
directly.

## Saving

- Create figures with `fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(...))` and pass
  `ax=ax` to seaborn, so each figure has a handle to save.
- Set the size before tuning text. Text that reads well on screen can be too
  small at column width.
- Prefer vector output, such as PDF or SVG, for line and text figures when the
  destination accepts it. Check the saved file for clipped labels.
- Close finished figures with `plt.close(fig)` in loops and scripts.
- In a Framework project, prefer `fw.save_figure(fig, "name")`.

writing.content:
---
name: writing
description: Use before writing or editing prose in a data analysis project, such as text about results, notebook text, captions, READMEs, and summaries of findings. Covers a plain register, numbers with their uncertainty, claims that match the design, and consistent names.
metadata:
  title: Writing
  summary: Plain, exact prose about data and findings.
---

# Writing

## Register

- Prefer plain declarative sentences with one claim each.
- Use bullets for parallel lists and paragraphs for arguments.
- Report null and unexpected results in the same register as expected ones.

## Numbers

- Use only numbers that come from the analysis output.
- State an estimate with its uncertainty, its units, and the sample it
  describes: "Mean systolic pressure was 4.2 mmHg higher in the treatment
  group (95% CI 1.8 to 6.6; n = 412)."
- Give counts with their denominators: "38 of 412 participants (9%)".
- Round to the precision the data supports, and use the same number of
  decimals for the same quantity throughout.
- Use "statistically significant" only about a test.

## Claims

- Use causal verbs such as "increased" and "caused" for randomized or
  explicitly causal designs.
- For observational associations, use "was associated with", "was higher
  among", or "differed by". Keep the same verbs in titles and summaries.
- Call an exploratory analysis exploratory.
- State a limitation once, specifically, where it applies: "Income was
  self-reported and missing for 14% of households."

## Names

- Call variables by what they measure, such as "household income". Use a
  column name such as `hh_inc_2` only when the reader needs to find it in the
  data.
- Give each group one name and keep it.
- Define an abbreviation at first use.
- Use the field's terms for statistical concepts.

## Wording

Prefer plain wording to these:

- Overselling, such as "striking", "remarkable", "clearly shows", and
  "proves".
- Openers such as "It is worth noting that" and "Interestingly".
- Narration of each step, such as "Now we load the data". Say what a step is
  for.
- Stacked hedges such as "may potentially suggest".

git-workflow.content:
---
name: git-workflow
description: Use when reviewing changes, committing analysis work, resolving merge conflicts, or coordinating branches in a research repository.
metadata:
  title: Using Git in an analysis project
  summary: Reviewable Git changes for analysis code and project files.
---

# Using Git in an analysis project

## Changes

- Check the branch, status, and diff before editing or committing.
- Keep unrelated work as it is.
- Stage explicit paths, so generated output, data, credentials, and
  machine-specific files stay out of commits.
- Keep each commit to one coherent change, and describe what changed.

## Conflicts

- Resolve notebook conflicts with notebook-aware tools when available.
- Regenerate generated files from their source.
- Rerun affected analyses after resolving a conflict.

## Shared history

- Leave shared history as it is. Check divergence before merging or rebasing.
- Commit, push, and publish only when the user asks.

jupyter-notebooks.content:
---
name: jupyter-notebooks
description: Use when creating or editing Jupyter notebooks, including kernel selection, execution order, reproducibility, and output review for R or Python.
metadata:
  title: Working in Jupyter notebooks
  summary: Notebooks that execute in order with the intended kernel.
---

# Working in Jupyter notebooks

## Editing

- Check the notebook's kernel and the project environment before editing.
- Edit notebooks with notebook-aware tools, which keep the JSON valid. Keep
  cell ids and metadata.

## Execution order

- Arrange cells in the order they run: setup and imports, data loading,
  transformations, analysis, and output.
- Keep text cells next to the results they explain.
- Restart the kernel and run all cells to confirm the notebook runs in order.
- Use project-relative paths, and set a seed when randomness affects reported
  results.

## Outputs

- Follow the repository's policy on keeping or clearing outputs.
- Save large data and binary outputs as files, and refer to them.
- Check outputs for credentials before sharing.
